title: Uniform Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Motion
lead: A ball moving round a circle at a steady rate casts a shadow that moves back and forth in simple harmonic motion. This section uses that projection to produce simple harmonic motion, and then reads the position, the speed and the period of any simple harmonic oscillator off the circle.
objectives: Compare simple harmonic motion with uniform circular motion.
summary_html: • A projection of uniform circular motion undergoes simple harmonic oscillation.
notes: The AP question and problems 2 and 4 have no answer in the book’s key and are left out.
exercise_notes: Bloom levels, concept tags and hints are AI-generated. Answers come from the book’s answer key; the AP question and problems 2 and 4 have no keyed answer and are left out. Numeric answers accept 2% tolerance.

figures.original_caption: The shadow of a ball rotating at constant angular velocity ω on a turntable goes back and forth in precise simple harmonic motion.

A point P moving on a circular path with a constant angular velocity ω is undergoing uniform circular motion. Its projection on the x-axis undergoes simple harmonic motion. Also shown is the velocity of this point around the circle, v_max, and its projection, which is v. Note that these velocities form a similar triangle to the displacement triangle.

exercises.prompt: Identify an object that undergoes uniform circular motion. Describe how you could trace the simple harmonic motion of this object as a wave.

answer.solution: A record player undergoes uniform circular motion. You could attach dowel rod to one point on the outside edge of the turntable and attach a pen to the other end of the dowel. As the record player turns, the pen will move. You can drag a long piece of paper under the pen, capturing its motion as a wave.

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the maximum velocity of an 85.0-kg person bouncing on a bathroom scale having a force constant of $1.50 \times 10^{6}\ \text{N/m}$, if the amplitude of the bounce is 0.200 cm? (b) What is the maximum energy stored in the spring?

parts.hint: Use $\kvmax = \kX\sqrt{\kk/m}$ with the amplitude in meters.
At the turning point all the energy is in the spring, $\tfrac{1}{2}\kk\kX^2$.

exercises.prompt: At what positions is the speed of a simple harmonic oscillator half its maximum? That is, what values of $\kx/\kX$ give $\kv = \pm\kvmax/2$, where $\kX$ is the amplitude of the motion?

answer.hint: Set $\sqrt{1 - \kx^2/\kX^2} = 1/2$ and solve for $\kx/\kX$. There are two positions, one on each side of equilibrium; give the positive one.
